extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and evaluating Markush-style patent claims that recite alternative members; explains when a Markush grouping is proper or improper and procedural steps for rejections and remediation. Intended to direct examiner practice and inform applicants how to respond or amend claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claim definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Markush' claim recites a list of alternatively useable members. The listing of specified alternatives within a Markush claim is referred to as a Markush group or Markush grouping. Claim language defined by a Markush grouping requires selection from a closed group 'consisting of' the alternative members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatment of claims reciting alternatives is not governed by the particular format used (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C' or 'A, B, or C'); any claim that recites alternatively usable members, regardless of format, should be treated as a Markush claim. See cited cases (Ex parte Markush; Abbott Labs v. Baxter; Amgen v. Amneal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Markush grouping requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping is proper only if the members of the group share a 'single structural similarity' and a common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two acceptable situations: (1) alternatives are all members of the same recognized physical or chemical class or the same art-recognized class and are disclosed or known to be functionally equivalent and have a common use; or (2) where alternatives are chemical compounds not in a recognized class, the members share both a substantial structural feature and a common use that flows from that feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single structural similarity — recognized class criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Members share a 'single structural similarity' when they belong to the same recognized physical or chemical class or to the same art-recognized class (i.e., the art expects members will behave the same way in the claimed context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The expectation is substitutability: each member could be substituted for another with the expectation the same intended result would be achieved (example: diaper fasteners). When a Markush group includes only materials from a recognized scientific or art-recognized class, the mere existence of the group tends to prove equivalence and can render the group unpatentable if one member is anticipated, absent convincing evidence of nonequivalency (In re Ruff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common use requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the Markush group must share a common function or use when disclosed in the specification or known in the art to be functionally equivalent in the context of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common use may be shown by the specification or prior art; absence of common use supports an 'improper Markush grouping' rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial structural feature route for chemical compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: If the listed chemical compounds are not members of a recognized class, a Markush grouping may still be proper if the alternatives share a substantial structural feature that is essential to a common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Harnisch, Hozumi): evaluate compounds as wholes to identify a common core/substantial structural feature (e.g., coumarin core) and whether that feature is disclosed as essential to the disclosed utility (e.g., dye activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate chemical compounds as wholes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Markush grouping defines alternative chemical compounds, the compounds must be considered as whole compounds and not broken down into elements or other components when assessing structural similarity and common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not focus on individual substituent moieties if the proper inquiry is whether the full compounds share the necessary common structure and use (citing Harnisch; In re Jones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush group in combination or process — substitutability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Markush grouping describes part of a combination or process, the members following an introductory phrase ('selected from the group consisting of', etc.) must be substitutable one for the other with the expectation that the same intended result would be achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-chemical combination/process contexts, the propriety hinges on functional substitutability for intended result (citing Multilayer Stretch Cling Film Holdings v. Berry Plastics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush grouping rejection procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner determines the species of a Markush group do not share a single structural similarity or common use, the claim may be rejected as containing an 'improper Markush grouping'. Such a rejection is on the merits and may be appealed to the PTAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form Paragraph 8.40 for improper Markush grouping rejections. The form paragraph should state why the alternatives fail the two-prong test and provide specifics (insert claim numbers, describe the improper Markush group(s), and explain why requirements are not met).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content required in improper Markush grouping rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An improper Markush grouping rejection must explain why the alternatives are not all members of the same recognized class and/or why they are not functionally equivalent and have a common use, and/or why (for chemical compounds) they do not share both a substantial structural feature and a related common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include bracketed specifics per Form Paragraph 8.40: claim numbers, description of Markush group(s), and the factual/legal reasons the group is improper. If election of species is appropriate, wait until after applicant has made an election before using this form paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing — compact prosecution and first-action requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An improper Markush grouping rejection should be made in the first action on the merits after presentation of the claim with the improper Markush grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means in the first Office action on the merits or the next Office action following presentation of the claim. If one or more claims include an improper Markush grouping, also require an election of an alternative or grouping of indistinct alternatives for search/examination if not previously made. Do not make a provisional election that includes the improper grouping before first merits action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner suggestions to overcome rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should include suggestions for how the applicant may overcome an improper Markush grouping rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested actions include proposing a proper Markush grouping based on the specification or requiring applicant to set forth each alternative (or grouping of patentably indistinct alternatives) in a series of independent or dependent claims. Examiner should not suggest any grouping that would clearly lack adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) when metes and bounds unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds of the Markush claim due to an inability to envision all members of the Markush grouping, the claim is indefinite and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a separate ground; see MPEP §2173.05(h) for related discussion. Rejection under improper grouping and 112(b) may both be appropriate where boundaries cannot be drawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of search/examination relative to proper grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: The search need not be extended to species that fall outside a proper Markush grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proper Markush grouping is identified, examiners limit search to the elected/selected species; see MPEP §803.02 for election/search practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining, overcoming, and reconsidering improper grouping rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An improper Markush grouping rejection should be maintained until the claim is amended to include only members sharing a single structural similarity and common use, or the applicant presents convincing arguments that the group members share such similarity and use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if applicant does not overcome the rejection, when all claims are otherwise in condition for allowance the examiner should reconsider the propriety of the rejection and withdraw it if warranted by the record and prior art. No Markush claim can be allowed until the improper grouping rejection is overcome or withdrawn and all other conditions satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of anticipation via class equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Markush group includes only members from a recognized scientific or art-recognized class of equivalent materials, the existence of the group tends to prove equivalence of its members, and if one member is anticipated in the prior art the group may be rendered unpatentable absent convincing evidence of non-equivalency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to In re Ruff and related precedent: actual equivalence is not sufficient to refuse patentability unless equivalence is disclosed in the prior art or is obvious under Section 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case evaluation and illustrative examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The propriety of Markush groupings must be decided on a case-by-case basis; examples (Harnisch, Dams, Hozumi, PCT example) illustrate application of the two-prong test and how to weigh common structural features and common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cited cases to guide factual analyses: focus on the commonality across alternative embodiments, the specification disclosure of common properties/utility, and whether the claimed feature is essential to the utility. Examples show how to apply principles when claims are broad or when alternatives vary in functional groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format neutrality of Markush treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment of claims reciting alternatives is not governed by the particular wording or format used to recite the alternatives; any claim that recites alternatively usable members should be treated as a Markush claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the alternatives are presented as a 'group consisting of', as 'A, B, or C', or in chemical formula form, the same substantive tests (single structural similarity and common use) apply.
